ch27.anchor: wash his hands in the golden basin
ch27.note: 'To wash one's hands in a golden basin' (金盆洗手) is the underworld's set ceremony of retirement: a man of the jianghu publicly renounces his violent trade and withdraws into respectable life, never to take it up again.

The 1842 treaty that ended the First Opium War and forced China to open Shanghai and other 'treaty ports' to foreign residence and trade. It is the legal root of the foreign concessions—the self-governing enclaves whose history this section traces.

A daotai (道台), or circuit intendant, was a senior Qing official ranking above the prefectures; the Shanghai daotai handled customs and the dealings with foreigners, and so negotiated the bounds of the early concessions.

The Small Swords Society (小刀会), a secret-society band that seized the walled Chinese city of Shanghai in an uprising from 1853. The disorder drove Chinese residents to shelter in the foreign settlements, the beginning of the mixed Chinese-and-foreign city the concessions became.

'Hong-Yang' names the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) by its two leaders, Hong Xiuquan and Yang Xiuqing. The vast civil war it loosed sent waves of refugees into the safety of the Shanghai concessions, swelling them into great cities.

The Gongbuju (工部局) was the Shanghai Municipal Council, the governing body of the International Settlement; the French Concession had its own separate council, the Gongdongju (公董局). Chen faults a newspaper for confusing the two.
